idiom_name: static const null instance with no-op overrides
implementation_notes: The classic realization is a small subclass of the interface whose every override returns a benign value or does nothing, plus one shared instance (a function-local static, a Meyers singleton, or a namespace-scope const) handed out wherever no real object exists. What replaces the pattern's machinery in modern C++ is the value-level alternative: std::monostate for an empty state inside a std::variant; plain std::optional is not a substitute because the caller still has to test it. Prefer the classic form when the interface is polymorphic and called from many sites, and accept the two costs: the special case must be completed whenever the interface grows, and its benign replies are invisible in the signature.
pitfalls: A function-local static is initialised thread-safely in C++11, but it is never destroyed in a controlled order: a special case with non-trivial members or a registering constructor can outlive the things it depends on.
A defaulted virtual body is easy to forget when the interface grows - the special case silently inherits the new no-op and callers silently get nothing.
Returning a reference extends the object's lifetime to the caller's use; returning a value sliced to the interface type loses the override, so know which one you are promising.

variants.name: std::monostate empty alternative in a std::variant
variants.implementation_notes: When the degenerate case is a state of a value rather than a missing collaborator, model it as an alternative instead of a subtype: std::variant<std::monostate, Config> is always default-constructible, and every visitor can handle the empty alternative explicitly. std::monostate is a unit type designed exactly for this role, so the special case needs no class of its own and the value stays copyable, comparable and trivially destructible. Choose it when the whole thing must remain a value type; stay with the classic null instance when callers should never see a variant at all.
pitfalls: Every visitor must handle std::monostate explicitly; with a generic lambda the empty branch is easy to miss and a wrong overload wins silently.
monostate means 'no value', not 'value missing for a reason': it cannot carry the partial information (the requested id, the failure kind) that an information-carrying special case keeps.
A valueless-by-exception variant (a throwing move) is a different state from a monostate alternative; code that treats both as 'empty' will misread the first.
